661.event_title: Churchill tells the Commons that Britain will fight on after Dunkirk
661.place: House of Commons, London, United Kingdom
661.event: After the evacuation of more than 338,000 Allied troops from Dunkirk, which had left much of the British Army's equipment behind in France, Prime Minister Winston Churchill reported on the war situation to the House of Commons on 4 June 1940. He warned that wars are not won by evacuations and prepared the country for a possible invasion. He declared that Britain would fight on the beaches, the landing grounds, the fields, the streets and the hills, and that it would never surrender.
661.explanation: At a moment when Britain's material strength was at its lowest, the speech made national resolve itself the country's main asset and helped carry Britain through the summer of 1940.
661.tie_back: The kural says that real firmness in action is firmness of mind and that every other kind of strength is something else, and Churchill rallied a nation that had just lost its army's equipment by appealing to its resolve rather than its resources.
661._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of resolve being treated as the decisive strength when material strength had failed; the speech expresses the resolve rather than proving it in action.

662.event_title: Cook's crew saves the Endeavour after it strikes the Great Barrier Reef
662.event: Around midnight on 10-11 June 1770 James Cook's ship HMS Endeavour struck a coral reef off the coast of what is now Queensland and began taking on water. Cook had the crew lighten the ship by throwing overboard around 40 to 50 tons of material, including ballast and six of its cannons, and the ship was hauled off the reef on a rising tide. The damaged ship was then taken to a river mouth, now the Endeavour River, where repairs took about six to seven weeks before the voyage continued.
662.explanation: Faced with the loss of the ship far from any help, Cook and his crew neither panicked nor gave up, and the expedition survived to complete its voyage.
662.tie_back: The kural's second rule of firmness is not to give way once harm has struck, and the Endeavour's crew kept working methodically after the grounding until the ship was saved.
662._accuracy_note: Illustrates only the second half of the kural (not yielding once harm has come); the first half, avoiding harm beforehand, is not shown, since the ship did strike the reef.

663.event_title: The secret evacuation of Anzac and Suvla at Gallipoli
663.event: After the failure of the Allied campaign at Gallipoli, a withdrawal plan devised largely by Lieutenant Colonel Brudenell White was carried out in stages and kept hidden from the Ottoman forces facing the Allied trenches. Periods of silence and irregular firing accustomed the enemy to quiet lines, men were taken off by night, and in the last hours self-firing drip rifles kept up occasional shots after the trenches were empty. About 36,000 troops left Anzac and Suvla over several nights ending on 20 December 1915 with very few casualties, and Helles was evacuated in the same way by 9 January 1916.
663.explanation: Because the plan stayed secret until it was complete, an operation that commanders had feared might cost heavy losses was achieved almost without loss of life, and it is often called the best-planned part of the whole campaign.
663.tie_back: The kural says true capability lies in carrying out a task so that it becomes known only when it is finished, and the Gallipoli withdrawal succeeded precisely because the enemy did not learn of it until the last troops had gone.
663._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of secrecy until completion; it is a specific, non-violent act within an otherwise costly war.

664.event_title: Kennedy's Moon goal is carried out as stated
664.event: On 25 May 1961 President John F. Kennedy asked a joint session of Congress to commit the United States to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth before the end of the decade. The goal required a huge national effort in funding, engineering and testing through the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo programmes. On 20 July 1969 Apollo 11 landed on the Moon, and its crew returned safely to Earth, within the deadline Kennedy had set.
664.explanation: Announcing the goal took one speech; meeting it exactly as stated took eight years of sustained work by hundreds of thousands of people.
664.tie_back: The kural says anyone can say how a thing should be done but doing it exactly as it was said is hard, and the Moon landing is a rare case of a public declaration fulfilled to the letter.
664._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of word made into deed exactly as stated, though Kennedy himself did not live to see it and the achievement belonged to a whole programme.

665.event_title: Engineer M. Visvesvaraya becomes Diwan of Mysore and later receives the Bharat Ratna
665.event: Mokshagundam Visvesvaraya joined the Mysore State service as Chief Engineer in 1909 and led work on the Krishnaraja Sagara dam, using automatic sluice gates of his own design; the dam created what was then one of the largest reservoirs in Asia. In 1912 the Maharaja's government made him Diwan of Mysore, a post he held until 1918, during which the dam project was given top priority. In 1955 he received the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honour, and his birthday, 15 September, is observed as Engineers' Day in India.
665.explanation: Visvesvaraya's record of carrying great works through to completion brought him first the ruler's trust and then the esteem of the whole nation.
665.tie_back: The kural says the firmness in action of the eminent reaches the king and so comes to be held in regard by all, and Visvesvaraya's proven firmness as an engineer won him the Maharaja's highest office and, later, national honour.
665._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of execution reaching the ruler and then winning general esteem; sources differ slightly on the exact sequence of the dam work and his appointment as Diwan.

666.event_title: The Eiffel Tower is completed in time for the 1889 Exposition
666.event: For the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centenary of the French Revolution, the organisers chose the design submitted by Gustave Eiffel's firm from more than 100 proposals. Construction began on 26 January 1887 and the tower was finished on 31 March 1889, in two years, two months and five days, with a small workforce and some 2.5 million rivets. It served as the entrance to the Exposition, which opened that May, and was visited by about two million people during the fair.
666.explanation: An unprecedented iron structure was built exactly to plan and on time, becoming a lasting symbol of engineering achievement.
666.tie_back: The kural says that planners who are firm in carrying out their plans attain what they aimed at in just the way they aimed at it, and Eiffel's team delivered the tower as designed and in time for the event it was built for.
666._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a plan carried out as conceived, though the sources speak of record speed rather than of a formally fixed deadline being met.

667.event_title: FC Barcelona signs the small thirteen-year-old Lionel Messi
667.event: As a boy in Argentina Lionel Messi was diagnosed with a growth hormone deficiency, and when his club there stopped paying for his treatment his family sought a club abroad. FC Barcelona's officials hesitated at first over his small size and the cost of the hormone therapy, but the club signed him and paid for his treatment when he arrived at the age of thirteen. He went on to become one of the most successful players in the club's history.
667.explanation: A player some thought too small became the centre of one of the greatest teams of his era, showing how misleading physical size can be as a measure of ability.
667.tie_back: The kural warns that no one should be scorned for small size, since the world has people like the little linchpin that holds a great chariot wheel, and Barcelona's decision not to judge the young Messi by his height gave the club its linchpin.
667._accuracy_note: A strong and close illustration of not despising someone for small stature; it is a sporting rather than a statecraft example.

668.event: In January 49 BCE the Roman Senate, led by Caesar's opponents, demanded that Julius Caesar give up his army and return to Rome as a private citizen. Caesar instead led his troops, reportedly a single legion, across the small river Rubicon, the boundary between his province of Cisalpine Gaul and Italy proper, an act that began a civil war. He then advanced rapidly through Italy, and the phrase crossing the Rubicon has since meant passing a point of no return.
668.explanation: Once Caesar had made his choice he acted at once and without hesitation, and the speed of his advance gave his opponents no time to organise.
668.tie_back: The kural says that once a course has been settled with a clear mind it should be carried out without wavering or delay, and Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon has become the world's shorthand for exactly such an irreversible, unhesitating commitment.
668._accuracy_note: A strong image of decisive commitment without wavering, though the decision led to civil war and the kural does not endorse the cause, only the manner of execution; exact dates are uncertain.

669.event_title: Junko Tabei reaches the summit of Everest after an avalanche
669.event: In 1975 Junko Tabei helped lead a Japanese all-women expedition to Mount Everest. While the team slept at Camp II, an avalanche struck their tents and knocked Tabei unconscious, but the expedition continued. On 16 May 1975 she became the first woman to reach the summit of Everest.
669.explanation: Tabei's climb opened the highest mountain to women climbers and showed what persistence could achieve after a near-fatal setback.
669.tie_back: The kural urges boldly carrying on with a task that brings joy in the end, even if much hardship comes along the way, and Tabei went on from being buried by an avalanche to a historic summit.
669._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of pressing on through severe hardship to a joyful end.

670.event_title: The Wright brothers fly days after Langley's well-funded Aerodrome fails
670.place: Potomac River, Washington, D.C., and Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, United States
670.event: Samuel Langley, Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, had government funding and great scientific prestige for his piloted Aerodrome, but it plunged into the Potomac on launch on 7 October 1903 and broke up again on 8 December 1903. His request for further funding was refused, he suffered public ridicule, and the project ended. Nine days later, on 17 December 1903, Wilbur and Orville Wright, bicycle makers who had worked on their machine through years of patient trials, made the first powered, controlled airplane flights near Kitty Hawk.
670.explanation: Prestige, money and official backing did not produce flight; the Wrights' persistent, methodical work did, and history credits them with the achievement.
670.tie_back: The kural says that whatever other strengths people have, the world does not value those who lack firmness in action, and the Wrights, with far fewer resources than Langley, won the lasting honour because they carried the task through.
670._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the contrast between resources and persistence fits, but Langley's work ended because funding was refused, not through any documented lack of resolve on his part.
